title: Prospective analysis of the impact of structured telephone preparation on the efficiency of newborn hearing screening depending on socioeconomic factors
summary:
Hearing tests in infants work best when the child is calm or asleep. In practice, this is not always the case, which can make the examination more difficult or time-consuming.

This study investigates whether a structured telephone preparation of parents before the appointment can help improve the efficiency of the examination. Some parents receive additional guidance on how to prepare their child.

The results may help to make future examinations faster and reduce the need for repeat visits.
conditions: Limited feasibility and efficiency of newborn hearing screening due to suboptimal examination conditions (e.g. awake or restless infant), which may lead to prolonged examination time or the need for repeat testing.

interventions.name: Standard care: Parents receive routine information during appointment scheduling (e.g. insurance card, referral, child health record). No structured preparation regarding the child’s sleep behavior prior to the examination is provided.

Intervention group I1: In addition to standard information, parents receive a structured telephone-based preparation prior to the examination. This includes specific instructions on sleep management of the child (e.g. maintaining wakefulness and adjusting sleep patterns) to optimize examination cond

Intervention group I2: Same as intervention group I1 (structured telephone-based preparation), with an additional reminder call 1–2 days prior to the examination to reinforce the preparation instructions.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Infants presenting for their first newborn hearing screening at the clinic and their legal guardians. Written informed consent from parents. Sufficient ability to communicate with the parents (with interpreter if necessary).
Exclusion criteria:
Severe underlying conditions of the infant (e.g. epilepsy as a contraindication for sleep deprivation, tracheostomy, active malignancy), acute infection on the day of examination, absence of a legal guardian able to provide consent, inability to communicate even with an interpreter, known familial hearing impairment with non-verbal communication, or technical issues preventing measurement.
